_about: Concept ladder for the Learn stage. One concept per rung. Rung ids are progress keys: never rename. skills are glossary.json ids that move to Practiced when the check is passed. goals maps checkpoint data-ids to the rungs (1-based) that teach them. lang: c programs are compiled and run to verify each check.

rungs.title: Update vs render
rungs.builds: The game loop and const pointers (Phase 4.5), the message loop and drawing a frame (Phase 5), and structs and passing by pointer and -> (Phase 3.5).
rungs.why: Every frame your game does two different jobs: decide what happened, then draw it. Keep them in separate functions and you can pause, slow down or debug one without touching the other. Mix them and every change breaks something.

parts: One job each

Every frame does two different jobs. update decides what happened: the player moved, an enemy stepped forward, a hit took a life. render draws the result. Keeping each function to one kind of work is called cohesion. When the picture looks wrong you open render, and when the score is wrong you open update. You never have to read both.
update is the only writer

Make one rule and keep it: only update changes the game. Input handling notes which keys are down, update acts on them, and render only reads. Give render a const Game* (the const pointers idea from Phase 4.5) and the compiler enforces the rule: a line like g->score = 0; inside render won't build.
State in a struct, not globals

Put everything that describes the game in one Game struct and pass its address. With twenty globals, any function might change any of them, so the rule above can't be checked. With a struct, the parameter list tells you: Game* can write, const Game* can't. Restarting gets easy too, because game_init(&g) refills the same struct.
Mistakes to avoid

• Moving an animation timer forward inside render. Pause no longer freezes it, and drawing twice makes it run double speed.
  • Drawing from inside update. Now you can't draw a frame without changing the game.
  • Skipping render while paused. The window stops repainting and looks frozen or blank.

walk: The whole game state lives in one struct: where the player is, and whether we’re paused. Here that’s just x and a flag.
update is the only function that changes the game. It takes a pointer so the change sticks (Phase 3.5).
render only reads. The const promise means the compiler stops you if you try to change g in here.
Frames 3 and 4 are “paused”. The || means “or”, so the flag is 1 on those two frames and 0 on the others.
Pause = skip update. If paused is 0, update runs and x moves.
Render runs every frame, paused or not, so the screen keeps drawing.
rungs.model: Mental model: a referee and a camera. The referee (update) decides what happened. The camera (render) only films it. Pausing the game sends the referee home but leaves the camera running.

check.q: What are the five lines this program prints?
check.hint: On frames 3 and 4 update is skipped. Is render skipped too?
check.why: Update runs on frames 1, 2 and 5, so x goes 10, 20, then 30. On the paused frames x stays 20, but render still runs and prints it. Skipping update froze the game, and rendering still drew it.

miss.0: That ignores the pause. On frames 3 and 4 update doesn’t run, so x doesn’t move.
miss.1: Only update is skipped when paused. Render is outside the if, so it prints on every frame.
miss.3: Nothing resets x. Skipping update just leaves it at 20.

tryit.task: Make the game pause properly: update only runs when not paused, but render always runs.

qa: Why not draw inside update?
Because then you can’t pause without freezing the picture too, and you can’t draw twice per update. Each function changes for its own reasons.
Why pass a pointer to update but const pointer to render?
update has to change the game, so it needs the real thing. render only looks, so const lets the compiler catch a mistake.
Does Godot do this too?
Yes. _process and _physics_process are where you update; the engine draws for you (or in _draw for custom drawing). Same split, different names.
What does one whole frame look like?

Input, then update, then render. handle_input() notes what the player pressed, update() moves things and checks hits, render() draws the result. Then the loop starts the next frame, about 60 times a second.
rungs.bridge: You can keep logic and drawing apart. Next: Delta time, so update moves things the same distance on a slow PC and a fast one.

rungs.title: Delta time: speed times dt
rungs.kick: dt · pixels per second · same speed at any fps
rungs.builds: Frame time with QueryPerformanceCounter (Phase 5), float and Division, remainder and casts (Phase 2).
rungs.why: If you write x += 5;, a PC running 144 frames a second moves the player more than twice as far as one running 60. Multiply by the frame time instead and the speed is the same on every machine.

parts: Per second, not per frame

Speeds in a game are written in pixels per second. Each frame you move by speed times dt, the seconds the last frame took. A fast PC runs more frames, each with a smaller dt, so after one second both machines have moved the same distance.
Getting dt right

In the real loop dt comes from frame time with QueryPerformanceCounter: the tick difference divided by the frequency. In the example it's 1.0f / (float)fps. The f matters: 1 / fps divides two ints, the whole-number division from Division, remainder and casts, and 1/60 is 0. Then every move is speed times 0.
float for speeds, double for the clock

A float keeps about 7 significant digits. That's plenty for a position on an 800-pixel screen. A running total isn't so lucky: after an hour, total += dt on a float is already rounding each frame noticeably, and after a day small frames barely change it at all. Keep the game clock in a double (about 15 digits) and keep dt and speeds as float.
Printing a float

printf("%f", x) works for a float because printf can't receive a float: C promotes it to double on the way in, and %f means double. There is no separate float code for printf. scanf is the odd one out, as you saw in scanf: there %f fills a float and %lf a double.
The f suffix under /WX

0.1 is a double. float dt = 0.1; makes MSVC warn (C4305, truncation), and /WX turns that into an error. It only fires when the value can't be stored exactly in a float: 120.0 and 0.5 fit, so they stay quiet, but 0.1 doesn't. Assigning a double expression to a float, such as x = x * 0.9;, warns as well (C4244). Put f on every float literal and you never have to think about which ones fit.

walk: This pretends to play one second of game at a given frame rate. speed is in pixels per second.

dt is the time one frame takes, in seconds: 1/30 at 30 fps, 1/60 at 60. Write 1.0f, not 1: 1 / fps is whole-number division and gives 0, so nothing would move. The (float) cast says you meant to turn fps into a float. In the real game you measure dt, as in frame time with QueryPerformanceCounter.
One second always contains fps frames, so the loop runs 30 times, or 60 times.
The key line. speed × dt is how far to move in this frame. Slow frames are long, so they move further. Fast frames are short, so they move less.
30 frames of a 1/30 second each: 120 pixels.
60 frames of a 1/60 second each: also 120 pixels. Same distance.
rungs.model: Mental model: paying by the hour, not by the visit. A fast PC visits more often, but each visit pays less, so you earn the same per hour.

check.q: Change line 5 to float dt = 1.0f / 60; (dt hard-coded as if every machine ran at 60 fps). What prints?
check.hint: The loop still runs fps times, but each step is now always 120 × 1/60. How many frames are in one second at each rate?
check.why: With dt stuck at 1/60, each step is 2 pixels. 30 frames × 2 = 60, and 60 frames × 2 = 120. The slower machine moved half as far in the same second. dt has to be the real frame time, not a guess.

miss.0: That only happens when dt matches the real frame time. A hard-coded dt gets the 30 fps run wrong.
miss.2: The 30 fps run takes only 30 steps of 2 pixels, which is 60.0, not 120.0.
miss.3: x is added to on every frame, not set. It keeps growing for the whole second.

tryit.task: Move the player 300 pixels per second using dt (seconds since the last frame).
tryit.answer: 300.0f * dt (the speed in pixels per second, times the frame time)

qa: Is dt always 1/60?
No, that’s the point. It’s whatever the last frame really took, so it wobbles a little. Use it as measured.
What if the game freezes for a second and dt becomes huge?
The player would leap across the level. Many games cap dt, for example at 0.05 seconds, so a hiccup can’t teleport anything.
Why f after 120.0?

120.0 is a double and 120.0f is a float. 120.0 happens to fit a float exactly, so MSVC is quiet there, but 0.1 doesn't, and MSVC warns (C4305), which /WX makes an error. Writing f every time saves you checking.
Why keep total time in a double when dt is a float?

dt is always small, so a float holds it well. A total keeps growing, and a float only keeps about 7 digits, so after an hour or so each tiny dt gets rounded as it's added. A double keeps about 15 digits, enough for days.
rungs.bridge: You can move things at a steady speed. Next: A state machine with next_state: menu, playing and game over, changed in one place.

rungs.title: A state machine with next_state
rungs.kick: next_state · change at the end of the frame · a name table
rungs.builds: State machines with enum and switch (Phase 4.5), enum (Phase 3.75), and designated initialisers from Phase 3.5.
rungs.why: Menu, playing and game over each behave differently, and you switch between them all the time. If you change state in the middle of a frame, later code in the same frame runs under the new state and things happen twice. Write the change into next_state and apply it at the very end.

parts: Change state at the end of the frame

In State machines with enum and switch (Phase 4.5) you assigned state the moment something happened. With a real frame (input, update, collisions, render) that bites. The player dies halfway through update, state becomes GAME_OVER, and the rest of the frame runs as GAME_OVER: the reset code clears the score before render draws the final one. The fix is one extra variable. Copy next_state = state at the top of the frame, write requests into next_state, and apply them in one line at the very end.
A name for every state

Printing state with %d shows 2, which tells you nothing. A table of names indexed by the enum fixes that. Writing [GAME_OVER] = "GAME_OVER" uses designated initialisers, the same idea as the named struct fields you met in Phase 3.5, but for array positions. Each name lands at its state's number however the enum is ordered, so adding PAUSED between PLAYING and GAME_OVER can't shift the others.
Why static const char *const

Read it right to left: an array of const pointers to const char. The first const means nobody can change the letters. The second means nobody can point an entry at a different string. static keeps the table private to this file. It never changes while the game runs, so let the compiler hold you to that.
Mistakes to avoid

• Setting state directly in one case and next_state in another. Pick next_state everywhere.
  • Adding a state at the end of the enum and forgetting its name. The table is too short and names[state] reads past its end. Ending the enum with a STATE_COUNT member and writing names[STATE_COUNT] keeps the size honest.
  • Resetting next_state halfway through the frame, which throws away a request.

walk: The same kind of enum as your Phase 4.5 state machine: MENU, PLAYING and GAME_OVER are the numbers 0, 1 and 2 underneath. The starter code adds an optional PAUSED.

A table of names, one per state. [PLAYING] = "PLAYING" puts each name at its state's index, so reordering the enum can't mix them up. static const char *const: private to this file, the letters can't change, and no entry can be pointed somewhere else.
At the top of every frame, next_state starts as “stay where we are”.
The switch looks at the current state and runs only that state’s code.
Frame 2 in MENU: we ask to go to PLAYING by setting next_state. The current state hasn’t changed.
This frame still prints the old state. Everything in the frame ran under one state.
The one place the state changes: the end of the frame. Next frame starts in the new state.
rungs.model: Mental model: finish the current turn before switching players. You write the next player’s name on a sticky note during your turn, and swap only once the turn is over.

check.q: What does the frame 2 line print?
check.hint: Line 12 sets next_state. When is state assigned from it?
check.why: next_state becomes PLAYING during frame 2, but state doesn’t change until line 21, after the printf. So frame 2 still prints MENU, and frame 3 is the first to print PLAYING.

miss.0: That would happen if line 12 changed state directly. It only sets next_state.
miss.1: GAME_OVER is only requested on frame 4, from PLAYING.
miss.2: The printf uses %s with the name from the list, so it prints text, not the number.

tryit.task: The player died. Request game over without switching in the middle of the frame.

qa: Why not just write state = GAME_OVER where it happens?
You can, and for tiny games it works. But anything below that line in the same frame now runs as GAME_OVER, which is where “it happened twice” bugs come from.
Can next_state be set more than once in a frame?
Yes, and the last one wins. That is usually fine. Decide which event should win if two can fire at once.
Why GameState and not State?
It matches the starter code and the Game struct, and it says whose state it is. Once there's an enemy state machine too, plain State would be ambiguous.
What does the table hold for a state I left out?
NULL. Printing NULL with %s is undefined behaviour, so give every state a name. MSVC happens to print (null), but don't rely on it.
rungs.bridge: You can change screens safely. Next: AABB collision, the four comparisons that tell you whether two boxes touch.

rungs.title: AABB collision
rungs.kick: two boxes · four comparisons · overlap on x and y
rungs.builds: Structs (Phase 3.5), and conditions with && and if (Phase 2.5).
rungs.why: “Did the bullet hit the enemy?” is really “do these two rectangles overlap?”. Four comparisons answer it. It’s the collision test behind pickups, enemies and platforms in your runner.

parts: Overlap on both axes

Two boxes hit when their ranges overlap on x and on y. On one axis that's two comparisons: A's left edge is left of B's right edge, and A's right edge is right of B's left edge. Do the same for top and bottom, join all four with &&, and you have the test.
&& stops early

C works through && left to right and stops at the first false (conditions, Phase 2.5). An enemy far to the right fails the second test and the y tests never run, so checking dozens of boxes a frame is cheap.
static inline for tiny helpers

inline asks the compiler to paste the body in where it's called instead of making a call; it's a hint, and a debug build (/Od) ignores it. static keeps the name private to the file. Together they also let a helper live in a header, which Splitting the game into files explains. The starter's aabb_overlap is these four comparisons on a Box with float fields, since positions move by speed * dt.
Tunnelling, and undoing the move

The test only sees where boxes are now. A bullet moving 40 pixels a frame can be left of a 20-pixel wall one frame and right of it the next: it tunnels through. Keep each move smaller than the thinnest thing it can hit, or split big moves into steps. To stop the player at a wall, save the old position, move, test, and put them back on a hit. Undo x and y separately and the player can slide along the wall.
Mistakes to avoid

• Storing right and bottom edges, then using them as width and height.
  • Switching to <= by accident: boxes that only touch now count as a hit.

walk: A box is its top-left corner (x, y) plus a width and height. Windows draws from the top-left too.

Returns 1 if the boxes overlap and 0 if they don't. All four conditions have to be true, so they're joined with &&. static inline marks it as a tiny private helper the compiler may paste in where it's called.
x axis: A’s left edge is left of B’s right edge, and A’s right edge is right of B’s left edge. Neither box is fully to one side.
y axis: the same test, up and down.
The player covers x 10 to 30 and y 10 to 30.
This box starts at x = 30, exactly where the player ends. Their edges meet but they don’t overlap, because a.x + a.w > b.x is 30 > 30, which is false.
rungs.model: Mental model: shadows. Two boxes touch only if their shadows overlap on the floor and their shadows overlap on the wall. If either shadow misses, there is no hit.

check.q: What do the four printed lines show, in order?
check.hint: Check each box against x 10 to 30 and y 10 to 30. Then look at whether edges that only meet count.
check.why: The corner box overlaps in both axes: 1. The touching box only meets at x = 30, and the test uses < and >, so 0. The far one misses: 0. The small one is entirely inside the player: 1. A box inside another still overlaps.

miss.1: Edges that only meet don’t count. a.x + a.w > b.x is 30 > 30, which is false, so the x test fails.
miss.2: A box completely inside another does overlap. Both axis tests pass.
miss.3: The corner box overlaps on both axes: x 25 to 45 meets 10 to 30, and y does too.

tryit.task: Finish the vertical half of the test.
tryit.answer: > and y: A’s bottom edge is below B’s top edge

qa: What if I want touching edges to count as a hit?
Change the four < and > to <= and >=. Most games leave them strict.
Why pass Box by value here?
It’s four ints, so copying is cheap and overlap can’t change the originals. Larger structs usually go by pointer.
Why test boxes instead of the real shapes?
Speed and simplicity: four comparisons instead of hundreds. Most games, Godot included, test boxes first and only check exact shapes when the boxes say maybe. Players almost never notice the corners.
Why static inline and not a plain function?

For one file, a plain function works just as well. static inline marks it as a tiny private helper, and it's the form that can sit in a header and be used from every .c file. The starter code's aabb_overlap does exactly that.
rungs.bridge: You can detect hits. Next: Text on screen, drawing the score in your Win32 window instead of the console.

rungs.title: Text on screen: TextOut
rungs.builds: WinMain, the window procedure, the message loop with PeekMessage and snprintf, and Combining flags with | and & (Phase 5); strings, strlen and Passing arrays to functions (Phase 3).
rungs.why: In the console you used printf. A Windows window has no console, so the score has to be drawn like everything else. TextOut draws a string at a position in the window, using the same device context you drew the rectangle with.

parts: Text is drawn like everything else

A window has no console, so the score is drawn like your rectangle: inside WM_PAINT, through the device context. Two steps: snprintf turns the number into text in a buffer (Copying and joining strings), then TextOut draws that many characters at a position. TextOut doesn't erase what was there, which is why a repaint clears the background first.
sizeof buf only works on an array

Inside WM_PAINT, buf is a real array, so sizeof buf is 32. Move the drawing into a helper like draw_label(HDC hdc, char *buf) and sizeof buf becomes 8, the size of a pointer, as Passing arrays to functions warned. snprintf would then cut every label to 7 letters. Pass the size as its own parameter.
TextOut is really TextOutA

windows.h has two of most text functions: TextOutA takes char strings and TextOutW takes wide ones. TextOut is a macro that picks one: if UNICODE is defined you get W, otherwise A. That's conditional compilation, the same trick as Preprocessor switches in Phase 4.5. build.bat never defines UNICODE, so plain "Score" strings work and the debugger shows TextOutA. A Visual Studio project defines UNICODE, which is why code copied from one uses L"Score".
A static score, and style bits

The score sits outside every function so WndProc can read it. Make it static, so no other .c file can reach in and change it (Static locals and globals). The window style WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW | WS_VISIBLE is two bit flags joined with |, straight from Combining flags with | and &.
MSVC notes
Drop the (int) in front of strlen and MSVC warns that converting size_t to int may lose data, which /WX turns into an error. The cast says the label is short and you know it.

walk: static: score lives outside every function so WndProc can see it, and static keeps it private to this file. In the prototype it moves into your Game struct.
Drawing belongs in WM_PAINT, the same place as your rectangle in Phase 5.
BeginPaint gives us the device context hdc, the surface we draw on.
snprintf builds "Score: 12" in buf and never writes past its 32 characters. sizeof buf is 32 here because buf is an array.

TextOut(hdc, x, y, text, length) draws at 10 across and 10 down. strlen counts the characters; the (int) cast is there because strlen returns size_t. Without UNICODE defined, TextOut is really TextOutA, the char version.
Always match BeginPaint with EndPaint.
The window set-up from Phase 5, cut down. WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW | WS_VISIBLE combines two style flags with |, as in Combining flags with | and &.
The PeekMessage loop from Phase 5. In the prototype, game_update and game_render go next to Sleep(16); here there is nothing to update, so the window only repaints when Windows asks.
rungs.model: Mental model: a label printer for your window. You give it the words, where to stick them, and how many letters to print.

check.q: You change the last TextOut argument from (int)strlen(buf) to 5. What appears in the window?
check.hint: The last argument is the number of characters to draw. Count “Score: 12”.
check.why: TextOut draws only the first 5 characters of buf: S, c, o, r, e. The string is 9 characters long, and the count tells TextOut where to stop.

miss.0: That needs a length of 9, which is what strlen gives.
miss.1: It still draws. A short length just cuts the text.
miss.2: The colon is the 6th character, so a length of 5 stops just before it. You’d need 6 to get “Score:”.

tryit.task: Draw “Lives: 3” from a variable called lives, at x = 10, y = 30.

qa: What is DrawText?
A cousin of TextOut that draws inside a rectangle, so it can centre or wrap text. TextOut is the simpler one to start with.
My text flickers when the score changes
That’s the redraw problem from Phase 5. Draw into a back buffer first (double buffering) and copy it to the window once.
Why is my score not updating?
WM_PAINT only runs when Windows asks. After changing the score, call InvalidateRect(hwnd, NULL, TRUE) so the window repaints.
Why does the debugger say TextOutA when I wrote TextOut?
TextOut is a macro. Without UNICODE defined it turns into TextOutA, the version that takes char strings. Call stacks and linker messages show the real name.
rungs.bridge: You can put the score on screen. Next: Splitting the game into files, so game.c and player.c each do one job.

rungs.title: Splitting the game into files
rungs.kick: one module per job · player_ prefix · static inline · SOURCES
rungs.builds: Header files and #pragma once, Linker errors (LNK2019) and static on functions (Phase 3.75), and Multiple files and LNK2005 (Phase 4.5).
rungs.why: The prototype has a loop, states, a player, collisions and a score. In one file, you and your partner edit the same lines all week and fight over merges. One file per job means you can work on player.c while your partner works on game.c, and every bug has an obvious home.

parts: One module, two files

A module is one job of the game in a .c file with its own .h. The header is the public face: types, prototypes and anything other files may use. The .c holds the bodies and the private details. For the prototype that means main.c (WinMain and the loop), game.c and game.h (the Game struct, the states, game_update, game_render) and player.c and player.h (movement and the Player struct). You split the runner once in Phase 4.5 to fix a problem. Now it's how every new piece starts.
Name prefixes

C has one shared pool of names for every public function and global, across all files. If game.c and player.c both define update, the linker finds two and stops with LNK2005. So prefix every public name with its module: player_update, game_update, enemy_spawn. You also always know which file to open. Enum constants share that pool too, which is why bigger projects write STATE_MENU, as in Phase 4.5.
The rules for each module

• Each .c includes its own header, so the compiler checks bodies against prototypes.
  • Helpers nobody else needs are static and stay out of the header.
  • A header includes what it uses: game.h includes player.h because Game holds a Player. Keep includes one way; player.h shouldn't include game.h.
  • Globals live in one .c, with an extern line in the header only if another file truly needs them. Usually it doesn't.
Tiny helpers: static inline

Sometimes a one-line helper like player_alive or aabb_overlap is wanted in every file. Three ways to put it in a header:

  • A normal function: every .c that includes it gets a full copy, and the linker reports LNK2005.
  • Plain inline: with no ordinary copy of the function anywhere else, gcc refuses to link it in a debug build, and the C standard allows that. MSVC may accept it. Don't rely on either; static inline is the form that works everywhere.
  • static inline: each .c gets its own private copy. Nothing clashes, nothing is missing.

A plain static function would also link, but every file that doesn't call it gets an unused copy, and MSVC can warn about an unused static function. static inline is the usual form.
Building it

build.bat lists every .c on the SOURCES line: set SOURCES=main.c game.c player.c, then cl %FLAGS% %SOURCES% /Fe:game.exe. Headers never go there. A new module is three steps: write the .h, write the .c, add the .c to SOURCES.
Mistakes to avoid

• Forgetting to add a new .c to SOURCES: LNK2019 for every function in it.
  • Defining a variable in a header: LNK2005.
  • Calling another module's static helper. The compiler can't see it, MSVC warns (C4013) and the link fails.
  • Two headers that include each other. Move the shared type into its own header.

walk: player.h is the module's public face: the Player type and what other files may call. Every public name starts with player_.
static inline: a one-line helper that lives in the header. Each .c that includes it gets its own private copy, so there is nothing for the linker to miss or find twice.
player.c includes its own header first, so the compiler checks every body against its prototype.
A private helper: static, and not in the header. No other file can call clamp_health, so another module can have its own.
The one real definition of player_heal. Only player.obj contains it.
main.c includes the header and nothing else from the player module. It never sees player.c.
player_alive needs no linking at all: main.c got its own copy through the include. Prints health 100, alive 1.
After the last line: build every .c together. In build.bat: set SOURCES=main.c player.c, then cl %FLAGS% %SOURCES% /Fe:game.exe. Headers never go in SOURCES.
rungs.model: Mental model: departments in a studio. Each has a front desk (the .h) and a back office (the .c). Other departments only talk to the front desk, and everyone at the player desk wears a player_ badge.

check.q: You forget player.c and build with set SOURCES=main.c. Which name does the linker complain about?
check.hint: Which of these does main.c call, and which ones did it get a copy of through the include?
check.why: main.c calls player_heal, whose only body is in player.c, so the linker reports LNK2019 for player_heal. player_alive is static inline in the header, so main.c compiled its own copy. clamp_health is never called from main.c at all.

miss.1: player_alive came in with the header. main.c has its own copy, so nothing is missing.
miss.2: Only player_heal lives in player.c. The static inline helper was pasted into main.c by the include.
miss.3: main.c never calls clamp_health. It's static and private to player.c, and nothing outside asks for it.

tryit.task: Put this one-line helper in enemy.h so every .c file can use it without a linker error.

qa: How do I decide what becomes a module?
One per thing you'd name in a sentence about the game: the player, the enemies, the game itself. main.c keeps only WinMain and the loop, calling game_init, game_update and game_render.
What happens with a plain inline in a header?

Standard C treats it as a hint with no real copy for the linker, so a debug build can fail to link with an unresolved symbol. gcc does; MSVC may let it through. Add static and each file has its own copy, on every compiler.
Why not make every function static inline in a header?
Every file then compiles its own copy, any change rebuilds every file, and the header fills with code. Keep it for helpers of one to three lines.
Can two modules have functions with the same name?
Only if both are static. Two public update functions give LNK2005. That's what the prefixes prevent: player_update and enemy_update never clash.
rungs.bridge: That's every concept in Phase 6. Next: The prototype build: wire states, movement, collision and the score into one window, split into game.c and player.c, with your partner.
